rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\text{molecular formula}=(\text{empirical formula})_{n},\qquad n=\frac{\text{molecular mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}$$
$$n(\text{element})=\frac{\%\text{element}}{100}\times\frac{1}{A_{\text{element}}};\qquad \text{divide all values by the smallest}$$
$$\text{mass of C}=\text{mass of }CO_{2}\times\frac{12}{44},\qquad \text{mass of H}=\text{mass of }H_{2}O\times\frac{2}{18}$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Empirical and molecular formula are the same for every compound. ✅ They coincide only when n = 1; for glucose the empirical formula is CH₂O but the molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆.  ·  ❌ The empirical formula can be found without the molecular mass. ✅ It can — but the molecular formula needs the molecular mass (or vapour density) to give n.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Glucose, fructose, formaldehyde, acetic acid and lactic acid all have the empirical formula CH₂O but different molecular formulas.  ·  Molecular mass from vapour density: M = 2 × VD (hydrogen reference).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** 0.2 g of an organic compound gives 0.44 g CO₂ and 0.18 g H₂O. Find the empirical formula. **Solution:** mass C = 0.44 × 12/44 = 0.12 g (0.01 mol); mass H = 0.18 × 2/18 = 0.02 g (0.02 mol); oxygen by difference = 0.2 − 0.12 − 0.02 = 0.06 g = 0.00375 mol. Divide by 0.00375 → C : H : O = 2.67 : 5.33 : 1 → ×3 → 8 : 16 : 3, so the empirical formula is C₈H₁₆O₃ — illustrating how careful the ratio step must be.  ·  **Problem:** An oxide of nitrogen contains 30.4% N and has VD = 46. **Solution:** N = 30.4/14 = 2.17, O = 69.6/16 = 4.35 → divide by 2.17 → 1 : 2, empirical formula NO₂, formula mass 46; n = 92/46 = 2 → molecular formula N₂O₄.

rows.text: Covers only: calculation of empirical, molecular formula from % composition, solving related numerical problems (within Stoichiometry).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning of the two formulas  ·  The **empirical formula** gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element present in a compound (CH₂O for glucose). The **molecular formula** gives the actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆ for glucose).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Modern instruments (CHN analysers and mass spectrometers) determine the empirical and molecular formula in minutes, but the arithmetic logic remains the same as the classical combustion-train method.  ·  1 mole = 6.022×10²³ entities (Avogadro constant, Nₐ). Molar mass (M) is g·mol⁻¹; for a compound M = Σ(atomic masses).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Learn the sequence exactly: percentage → mass → moles → divide by the smallest → whole numbers → n → molecular formula.  ·  Never leave a fractional ratio; multiply to whole numbers before computing the formula mass.

rows.text: n (mol) = mass/M = volume(ideal gas, STP)/22.4 L = N/Nₐ.  ·  Limiting reactant is the one consumed first; % yield = (experimental/theoretical)×100.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Standard procedure from percentage composition  ·  (1) Take the percentage of each element as its mass in 100 g of the compound. (2) Divide each mass by the atomic mass of that element to obtain the number of moles. (3) Divide all the mole values by the smallest one.…  ·  ### 3. Worked example (percentage composition)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: n = m / M  ·  n = V / 22.4 (g at STP)  ·  % yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ A ratio of 1 : 1.5 is acceptable as an empirical formula. ✅ Ratios must be whole numbers, so multiply by 2 to obtain 2 : 3.  ·  ❌ Oxygen must always be estimated directly. ✅ In combustion analysis oxygen is normally found by difference (total mass − mass of C − mass of H).  ·  ❌ Two compounds with the same empirical formula are the same substance. ✅ They may be isomers or entirely different compounds with different molecular masses.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ entities (avogadro constant, nₐ). molar mass (m) is g·mol⁻¹; for a compound m = σ(atomic masses)..  ·  Remember the by-difference rule for oxygen and the conversion factors 12/44 for carbon and 2/18 for hydrogen.  ·  A compound contains 40% C, 6.67% H and 53.33% O and has molecular mass 180. Determine its empirical and molecular formula.

rows.text: 0.2 g of an organic compound on combustion gives 0.44 g CO₂ and 0.18 g H₂O. Find its empirical formula.  ·  An oxide of nitrogen contains 30.4% nitrogen and has vapour density 46. Find its molecular formula.  ·  A hydrated salt contains 36.1% water of crystallisation and its anhydrous salt has molar mass 120 g mol⁻¹. Find the number of water molecules per formula unit.
